options: Use RDMA READ instead of WRITE
Register one large pool at startup, preferably on huge pages, and reuse buffers from it
Disable the protection domain
Use more QPs
explain: Registration enters the kernel and pins pages, so per-request registration puts the slow control path back on the data path. Registering a pool once fixes that, and large pages keep the NIC's translation cache small (FaRM's lesson).

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Scaling RDMA: NIC caches, doorbells, timeouts and failure
question: Your RC QP has `timeout = 14` and `retry_cnt = 7`. A peer machine loses power mid-transfer. What does the sender see, and roughly when?
options: Nothing; the WR stays pending forever
An IBV_WC_RETRY_EXC_ERR completion after on the order of half a second, with the QP in an error state
An RNR error immediately
A TCP reset
explain: With no ACKs, the NIC retries after each 67.1 ms timeout; once retry_cnt is exhausted the WR completes with IBV_WC_RETRY_EXC_ERR (about 8 x 67 ms = 537 ms in the simple model). RNR is about missing receive buffers on a live peer, not a dead one.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Delta-encoded state and choosing the transport
question: A Colyseus room has 200 entities and you call `sort()` on their ArraySchema every tick to keep a leaderboard ordered. Bandwidth spikes. Why?
options: Sorting changes refIds, which forces a full resync
Schemas cannot hold more than 63 entities
sort() marks every index as changed, so the whole array is re-sent every patch
Sorted arrays disable delta encoding for the whole room
explain: The Colyseus optimization docs: sort() re-sends every element because every index is marked changed. Sort a plain copy on the client, or sort a separate array of indexes, instead.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Implicit feedback: preference, confidence and weighted ALS
question: Why does the identity Y^T C^u Y = Y^T Y + Y^T (C^u - I) Y matter?
options: It makes the loss convex in X and Y jointly
It lets each user update cost depend on that user's n_u touched items instead of all n items, so a sweep is linear in the number of non-zeros
It removes the need for regularization
It turns ALS into SGD
explain: Y^T Y is shared and precomputed once per sweep. The user-specific correction only involves rows with c_ui different from 1, which are the items the user touched.

courseTitle: Measuring size from a reference marker
lessonTitle: Why one pixels-per-mm ratio fails on a tilted photo
question: When is a single pixels-per-mm ratio from the card exact for an object on the same table?
options: Whenever the card and the object are both fully visible
When you average the ratios from all four edges
When the image plane is parallel to the table, so every table point has the same depth
When the object is shorter than the card
explain: With the camera looking straight at the plane, every point on it has the same Z, so f/Z is one constant. Averaging edges or keeping the object short reduces nothing about perspective; only a fronto-parallel view makes the ratio constant (ignoring lens distortion).

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: When each join wins: row counts, probes and memory
question: Which input should a hash join normally build its hash table on?
options: The larger input, so probing is cheaper
Whichever comes first in the FROM clause
The input that is already sorted
The smaller input, so the table fits in memory
explain: Build cost and memory grow with the build side, while each probe is a constant-time lookup either way. Building on the smaller input keeps the table in memory and avoids batching. In the docs' plan the Hash node sits over the 100-row tenk1 scan, not the 10000-row tenk2.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Leaderless quorums: why R + W > N makes reads overlap writes
question: N = 5 with R = 4, W = 2. Reads always overlap the last write, yet two clients writing the same key at the same time can both succeed without either write reaching a replica that has the other. Why?
options: Because R + W = 6 is too close to N
Because W = 2 is not a majority of 5, so two write sets can be disjoint
Because reads with R = 4 cannot tolerate failures
Because coordinators send writes to only W replicas
explain: Read/write overlap needs R + W > N. Write/write overlap needs 2W > N. Two sets of 2 fit disjointly inside 5 replicas, so concurrent writers cannot detect each other through a shared replica.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: When a high score stops meaning a solved task
question: Which of these is NOT reward hacking?
options: An agent edits the unit tests so they pass without fixing the bug
A robot moves between the camera and the object so a learned reward model thinks it grasped it
A model fails a coding task because it cannot write the algorithm, and gets reward 0
A boat circles to re-collect shaping points instead of finishing the race
explain: Reward hacking requires a high proxy score with poor true performance. A model that honestly fails gets a low proxy score that matches its true performance: that is a capability gap, not a specification failure.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: Catching hacks: CoT monitors, obfuscation, generalization
question: Your team's CoT monitor flags 5 percent of training rollouts as hacking. A teammate proposes subtracting reward whenever the monitor fires. Based on Baker et al., what is the main risk?
options: The monitor will become more accurate over time and over-penalize
GRPO cannot use non-binary rewards
After enough optimization the agent may keep hacking while writing CoTs that no longer reveal it, so the 5 percent signal drops without the hacking stopping
The model will stop producing a chain of thought
explain: In their experiment, the CoT-pressured agent hacked less early on but later hacked at a significant rate with monitor recall near zero. A falling flag rate would then look like success while hiding the problem. Using the monitor to find and patch environment bugs keeps the signal.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Weight sync: resharding and moving the bytes every step
question: A disaggregated run broadcasts a 70B BF16 model (140 GB) from one trainer rank over a single 400 Gb/s NIC every step. Roughly how long is the transfer at line rate, and what is the cheapest big improvement?
options: 0.35 s; nothing to improve
2.8 s; send disjoint shards from many trainer ranks in parallel so many NICs carry the load
28 s; switch to FP32 to avoid conversions
280 s; checkpoint to shared storage instead
explain: 140 GB at 50 GB/s is 2.8 s. The transfer is limited by one NIC. Sending shards from many trainer ranks in parallel (8 NICs gives 0.35 s), shard-to-shard resharding, or overlapping the sync with generation all help; FP32 doubles the bytes.

courseTitle: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
lessonTitle: Ceilings, hierarchical rooflines and Nsight Compute
question: Nsight Compute shows a kernel's L1, L2 and DRAM points almost on top of each other, sitting on the DRAM slope. What is the best next step?
options: Switch to Tensor Cores to raise the flat roof
Restructure for reuse (tiling, fusion) so fewer bytes reach DRAM
Nothing: being on the DRAM roof means it is already optimal
Raise the clock frequency to move the ridge point left
explain: Overlapping points mean almost every byte touched in L1 also came from DRAM: no reuse. The kernel is on the DRAM roof at its current intensity, so the way up is to raise intensity by reusing data in shared memory or registers, or by fusing with neighbors. A higher flat roof does nothing for a memory bound kernel.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: MTTR: detect, triage, mitigate, resolve
question: A team reduced detection from 8 minutes to 1 by alerting on every service's CPU, queue depth and pool wait. Their mean time to resolution got worse. What most likely happened?
options: Detection and triage are independent, so this cannot happen
More alerts means more deduplication work in Alertmanager, which delays notification
Cause-based alerts detect faster but page more often and from more places, so the alert storm grew and triage took longer than the detection saved
Alerting on saturation is always wrong
explain: Cause-based alerting trades triage time for detection time, and the trade is often bad: every service that is merely a victim now pages too. The SLO-based pattern is to page on the symptom your users feel and keep the cause-level signals as unpaged context, which is exactly what lesson 1 did with 9 groups and 1 page. Saturation signals are valuable; paging a human on each of them is the problem.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Ties, missing documents and the window size
question: Your fused results flicker between two orders on repeated identical requests. Which fix addresses the most likely cause?
options: Increase k
Add an explicit tie-break (best single rank, then document id) after sorting by RRF score
Normalize scores with min-max before RRF
Switch to CombSUM
explain: Exact RRF ties are frequent (any two documents with the same multiset of ranks). Without an explicit secondary key their order depends on hash or arrival order. Changing k changes which documents tie but does not remove ties.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Pinning: building kernel objects where they will live
question: Which struct field must be declared with `#[pin]` and initialized with `<-`?
options: `count: u64`
`name: &'static CStr`
`state: Mutex<State>`
`buf: KVec<u8>` (the vector's heap buffer may be reallocated)
explain: The `Mutex` wraps a C `struct mutex` that the kernel requires to stay at the address it was initialized at, so it is pinned and built in place with `new_mutex!`. A `KVec` may move its *buffer* on growth, but the KVec struct itself (pointer, length, capacity) can be moved freely.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Dispatch queues: how tasks travel from BPF to a CPU
question: Your enqueue callback calls scx_bpf_dsq_insert_vtime(p, SCX_DSQ_GLOBAL, slice, vtime, flags). What happens?
options: Tasks are kept in vtime order inside the global DSQ
The vtime is ignored and the task is appended FIFO
It is an error: built-in DSQs do not support priority-queue insertion, so you need a custom DSQ
The task is silently moved to the caller CPU's local DSQ
explain: Built-in DSQs (local and global) are FIFO only. The docs and scx_simple's comments say vtime insertion needs a DSQ created with scx_bpf_create_dsq(); invalid use is reported as a scheduler error, which unloads it.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Why a model can teach itself: improve, then distill
question: After three rounds in the toy, move d has prior 0. Suppose d was actually the best move and its value estimate was wrong. What happens in later rounds without exploration noise?
options: d is never visited, because its exploration bonus is P(d) times something, which is 0, and its Q stays 0
800 simulations are enough that the search reaches d eventually
The value loss on z will raise P(d) automatically
The gate at 55% will reject the network and restore d
explain: The pUCT bonus is proportional to the prior. With P(d) = 0 and an unvisited Q of 0, d never has the highest score, so the search never looks at it and the outcome z never reflects it. This is exactly why AlphaZero adds Dirichlet noise to the root prior during self-play.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Inventing the tasks: Absolute Zero and what bounds every loop
question: A team wants a model to improve its customer-support replies, has thousands of real customer questions, and has no answer key or human preference labels. Which loop fits, and what is the main risk to monitor?
options: ReST-EM with a binary correctness reward; the risk is overfitting a small problem set
AlphaZero-style tree search; the risk is lack of exploration noise
Absolute Zero; the risk is nondeterministic programs
Self-Rewarding with the model as judge; the risk is the policy exploiting the judge, for example by growing longer replies
explain: Without checkable answers, the options are a judge or a human target. Self-Rewarding needs only prompts and a seed of judging examples. Its documented risk is that the judge's biases get amplified: the paper itself saw average response length grow about 2.3x over two iterations and flagged reward hacking.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Scaling out: TP, DP, DP attention, EP and cache-aware routing
question: You serve a DeepSeek MLA model on 8 GPUs with tensor parallelism 8 and see far fewer concurrent requests than the KV memory should allow. What explains it, and what helps?
options: The radix tree uses too much CPU memory; disable it
MLA's single latent KV is replicated on every TP rank; enabling DP attention keeps each request's KV on one GPU
The chunked prefill size is too large; set it to 512
Expert parallelism duplicates the KV cache; lower `--ep-size`
explain: TP shards attention by heads, and MLA has no per-head KV to shard, so every rank stores the full cache. DP attention (`--attn-dp-size`) partitions requests instead, cutting duplication.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Bidirectional search and contraction hierarchies
question: After contraction, an important motorway is closed and its weight becomes very large. What happens to a plain CH built for the old weights?
options: Queries remain correct, since shortcuts are recomputed during each query
Shortcuts that include the motorway now carry stale weights, so the contraction (at least the weights) must be redone
Only the node order must change; shortcut weights update themselves
Nothing changes, because CH queries ignore original arc weights
explain: Shortcut weights are sums of original arc weights fixed at preprocessing time. The survey notes CH can keep its node order and rerun contraction for a new metric, but some recomputation is unavoidable. Handling frequent weight changes cheaply is what customizable methods target (next lesson).

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: The FFT: from N squared to N log N with butterflies
question: How many butterflies does a radix-2 FFT of N = 8 samples perform?
explain: There are log2 8 = 3 stages and each stage has N/2 = 4 butterflies, so 12 in total. 64 is the number of multiply-adds in the direct DFT (N squared), and 24 is N log2 N, which counts outputs over all stages (8 per stage), two per butterfly.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Why speedups fall short: latency chains and the memory wall
question: Your Neon float sum with one accumulator runs exactly 4x faster than scalar, never more, even on data in L1. What is the most likely next step?
options: Use 4 to 8 independent accumulators and combine them at the end
Switch to 512-bit vectors
Align the array to 64 bytes
Add -O3
explain: Both the scalar and the 1-accumulator loops are bound by add latency: one add per chain per latency period. Independent accumulators overlap the chain; on the measured M5 Pro that took 4.5x to 15.5x.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Shipping SIMD: -march levels, runtime dispatch, portability
question: A loop over an array of 64-byte structs reads one float field per struct. AVX2 intrinsics give almost no speedup. What is the most effective first change?
options: Use AVX-512 instead
Store that field in its own contiguous array (struct-of-arrays) so one load brings 8 useful floats
Add more accumulators
Use target_clones
explain: With array-of-structs, each useful float sits 64 bytes from the next, so a vector needs a gather or 8 separate loads and wastes most of each cache line. A separate float array gives contiguous vector loads and 16 floats per cache line.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: How Linux stacks them, and how to choose
question: A game allocates thousands of temporary objects while building each frame, and none of them is needed after the frame is drawn. Which allocator fits best?
options: A buddy allocator, so the temporary objects can merge back into big blocks
A slab cache per object type, so each object can be freed individually
The general-purpose malloc, because the objects have different sizes
A per-frame bump arena that is reset after the frame is drawn
explain: All objects share one lifetime that ends at a known point, which is exactly the phase-oriented pattern bump allocation is built for: each allocation is a pointer add and freeing the whole frame is one reset.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Generating data: the rollout loop and your own functions
question: Your agent calls a code interpreter between model turns and appends the interpreter output to the response. Training loss starts rewarding the model for "predicting" interpreter output. What is the bug?
options: The reward function should return a list
You need --rollout-function-path instead of a custom generate function
The router should be bypassed for tool calls
Tool output tokens were appended with trainable=True instead of trainable=False, so they are in the loss mask
explain: Only model-generated tokens should carry loss. The search-r1 example appends observation tokens with `trainable=False` (loss mask 0). Swapping hook types does not fix a wrong mask.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: The sparse autoencoder: a wide, sparse dictionary for activations
question: You train an SAE on layer 6 residual-stream activations of your GPT. Which statement is true?
options: The GPT's weights are updated so its neurons become monosemantic
The SAE has fewer hidden units than d_model so it compresses the activations
The SAE is trained on next-token cross-entropy only
The GPT is frozen; the SAE learns a wider, sparse re-description of the saved layer 6 vectors
explain: The SAE is a separate model trained on stored activations. It is overcomplete (M much larger than d) and trained with a reconstruction plus sparsity objective, not by changing the language model.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Six sensors and a blank map: interpolation as weighted averaging
question: A colleague says nearest neighbor is safest because it never invents values that were not measured. What is the main weakness of the resulting map?
options: It cannot be computed without a fitted variogram
It is discontinuous: the value jumps at Voronoi cell borders even when the true field is smooth
It always returns the global mean far from sensors
It gives every sensor the same weight
explain: Nearest neighbor copies the closest reading, so the map is a set of flat Voronoi tiles with steps at the borders. It needs no model, and far from sensors it still copies the nearest one rather than the mean.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Which map to trust: leave-one-out cross-validation
question: You have 5,000 weather stations and need a 1 km map nightly. Global ordinary kriging is too slow. Which change keeps most of kriging's benefits?
options: Switch to nearest neighbor
Krige from a local neighborhood of the nearest few dozen stations per target, using a variogram fitted once on all stations
Drop the variogram and set all weights to 1/5000
Use IDW with p = 0
explain: Local neighborhoods (like scikit-gstat's max_points or RBFInterpolator's neighbors) make each solve small. Distant stations get negligible weight beyond the range anyway, so the map changes little while cost drops sharply.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: How many tokens per round, and what speedup to expect
question: Which change raises the maximum achievable speedup when the draft is free (c = 0)?
options: Increasing gamma beyond 20
Lowering the target's temperature has no effect
Using a bigger GPU for the draft
Raising alpha, because the speedup is capped by 1/(1 - alpha)
explain: With c = 0 the speedup is the expected tokens per pass, bounded by 1/(1 - alpha) however large gamma gets. Only better acceptance raises the cap; lower temperature usually helps because it sharpens both distributions.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Whisper: a transformer over 30-second spectrogram windows
question: Whisper's timestamp tokens are quantized to the native resolution. A word starts at 1.234 s. What is the closest timestamp the model can emit?
explain: Each encoder position covers 20 ms (30 s / 1500), and timestamp tokens are on the same 20 ms grid: ..., 1.22, 1.24, ... The nearest grid point to 1.234 s is 1.24 s. Finer word timings need extra machinery, such as the cross-attention alignment the openai/whisper code offers for word timestamps.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The heap: free lists, chunk headers and where malloc gets memory
question: On 64-bit glibc, how many heap bytes does `malloc(25)` consume?
explain: request2size computes (25 + 8 + 15) rounded down to a multiple of 16 = 48. The 8-byte header pushes 25 bytes past the 32-byte minimum chunk, whose usable size is only 24.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Steering by adding a vector to the residual stream
question: What does ActAdd need in order to build a steering vector?
options: A labeled dataset of a few thousand examples and a few gradient steps
A trained linear probe on the target concept
One pair of contrasting prompts and two forward passes
Access to the model's training data
explain: ActAdd is optimization-free: two forward passes on a prompt pair such as Love and Hate, a subtraction, and a scale factor. CAA, ITI (developed independently of ActAdd, slightly earlier) and RepE's reading vectors use more examples to get a cleaner direction; none of these fine-tunes the model.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Side effects and how to evaluate a steering vector
question: Why is a random vector of the same norm a necessary baseline?
options: To check the hook is installed
Because random vectors are always better at steering
To show the effect comes from the direction and not from merely perturbing the stream by that much
To estimate the residual stream norm
explain: Any large perturbation changes outputs somewhat. ActAdd and ITI both compared against random directions (ITI's random direction moved TruthfulQA from 30.5% to only 31.2%) to show their direction specifically carries the concept.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Downsampling, retention and exactly-once vs at-least-once
question: Your sink appends one row per window firing. With allowed lateness 5 s, window [0,10) fires at count 4 and later at count 5. A dashboard sums all rows per window. What goes wrong and what fixes it?
options: The window is counted as 4 + 5 = 9 readings; write with an upsert keyed by (sensor, window) since firings are accumulating
Nothing; the second firing contains only the late reading
Late firings are never sent to sinks
The fix is to set allowed lateness higher
explain: In accumulating mode each firing is the full refined result, so appending both rows double counts. Overwrite by window key, or use discarding mode and have the consumer add deltas, or emit retractions.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Causal masks, cross-attention and multiple heads
question: With d_model = 512, how many parameters are in the four projection matrices (W^Q, W^K, W^V for all heads, plus W^O) of one multi-head attention layer, ignoring biases?
explain: Each of W^Q, W^K, W^V is 8 heads x (512 x 64) = 512 x 512 in total, and W^O is 512 x 512. That gives 4 x 512^2 = 1,048,576 weights. Splitting into heads does not multiply the parameter count.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Term-frequency saturation: what k1 controls
question: A product search team sees titles like "usb cable usb-c usb charger usb" outranking clean titles for the query usb. Which change to k1 most directly reduces the benefit of repeating a word?
options: Increase k1 from 1.2 to 5
Set b to 0
Decrease k1 from 1.2 to about 0.5
Leave k1, since BM25 already ignores repeats
explain: Lower k1 makes the factor saturate sooner, so the second and later copies add less. Raising k1 does the opposite. b controls length normalization, not repetition. BM25 does not ignore repeats; with k1 = 1.2 the fourth copy still adds weight.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Causal self-attention: each position may only look backward
question: Why does nanoGPT compute q, k and v for all 12 heads with one 768-to-2304 Linear instead of 36 small ones?
options: It is mathematically different and gives better accuracy
GPT-2 heads share their key matrices
It halves the parameter count
One large matrix multiply uses the GPU far better than many small ones, and gives the same result
explain: Stacking the per-head projection matrices side by side is the same linear map, so the outputs are identical. The gain is purely efficiency: one large matmul instead of many small launches. Parameter count is the same 768 x 2304 weights either way.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: A derivative is the slope you see when you zoom in
question: A loss $L(w)$ has derivative $L'(w) = -4$ at the current weight. Which small change to $w$ lowers the loss?
options: Decrease w, because the derivative is negative
Increase w slightly: the slope is negative, so L falls as w grows
Neither: a negative derivative means you are at a minimum
Any change, because the loss is already decreasing over time
explain: A negative slope means $L$ goes down as $w$ goes up, so a small increase in $w$ lowers $L$ by about $4$ times the step. A minimum is where the derivative is zero, not negative.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: how bash really runs your commands
lessonTitle: What happens when you press Enter: lookup, fork, exec, wait
question: You type `deploy` and get `command not found` with status 127, yet `ls ~/bin/deploy` shows the file exists and is executable. What is the most likely cause?
options: The file needs a .sh extension
Exit status 127 means the program crashed while starting
`~/bin` is not one of the directories in PATH
Bash only searches PATH for builtins
explain: Names without a slash are only looked up in the PATH directories. Add the directory to PATH or call it by path, `~/bin/deploy`. Extensions mean nothing to the kernel, and a crash would give a different status.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: how bash really runs your commands
lessonTitle: Exit statuses and scripts that fail loudly
question: A CI step runs `pytest | tee test.log` and always shows green even when tests fail. What is the minimal fix?
options: Replace `|` with `&&`
Add `set -u`
Add `set -o pipefail` before the command
Redirect with `2>&1` instead of piping
explain: The pipeline's status is tee's, which succeeds. pipefail makes the pipeline report the rightmost non-zero status, so pytest's failure surfaces. `&&` would stop tee from seeing the output stream at all.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: What the geometry means: cosine, analogies and PMI
question: A teammate reports that *king - man + woman* returns *king* in your system. What is the best first check?
options: Retrain with a larger dimension
Switch from cosine to Euclidean distance
Whether the nearest-neighbour search excludes the three query words, as the original evaluation did
Increase the number of negative samples
explain: Returning an input word is the expected behaviour when inputs are not excluded: Nissim et al. measured 0.21 accuracy unconstrained vs 0.74 constrained on the same vectors.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: The KV cache: why memory grows with every token
question: A team switches a model from 32 KV heads to 8 (GQA), keeping everything else. What changes most directly?
options: KV cache per token shrinks 4x, so more or longer sequences fit and decode reads fewer cache bytes
Weights shrink by 4x
Prefill FLOPs drop 4x
Context length must be cut by 4x
explain: Only the key and value projections shrink, which are a small part of the weights. The cache stores 8 instead of 32 heads per layer, a 4x reduction in KV memory and KV traffic.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Where a program's memory lives: code, heap and stack
question: Right after `call square` executes, which statement is true?
options: rsp increased by 8 and the program counter points at square
rsp is unchanged; the return address is kept in a special register
rsp decreased by 8, the stack top holds the address of the instruction after the call, and the program counter points at square
rsp decreased by 8 and the stack top holds the address of square
explain: The stack grows down, so a push subtracts 8 from rsp. call pushes the return address (the next instruction in the caller), not the target, then jumps by writing square's address into the program counter.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: From text predictor to assistant: the three-stage recipe
question: Roughly what fraction of GPT-3's pretraining compute did the 175B InstructGPT PPO-ptx run use?
options: About 50 percent
About 16 percent
About 1.6 percent
About 0.01 percent
explain: 60 / 3,640 is about 0.0165, so about 1.6 percent. The scarce input for alignment is human data (demonstrations and comparisons), not compute.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: RL with PPO: maximize reward, stay close to the SFT model
question: Why does InstructGPT keep a frozen copy of the SFT model during RL?
options: To generate the training prompts
To replace the reward model when it is uncertain
To compute log-probabilities for the KL penalty that anchors the policy
To serve as the value function
explain: The frozen SFT model supplies log pi_SFT for every sampled token, which the per-token KL penalty compares with the policy's log-probabilities. The value function is a separate model initialized from the reward model.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Answering AND queries by merging postings
question: Why does the engine keep df in the in-memory dictionary even for a pure Boolean search engine?
options: Boolean retrieval multiplies scores by df
It lets the planner order terms by list length before reading any postings
The merge algorithm needs df to know when to stop
It is needed to decompress postings
explain: Knowing each list's length up front lets the query optimizer intersect the shortest lists first. The merge itself stops when either pointer runs off its list, so it never needs df.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: From main.c to a running program: the four toolchain stages
question: What does `gcc -c main.c` produce?
options: An executable called a.out
Preprocessed C text on standard output
An object file main.o with unresolved references to area and printf
Assembly code in main.s
explain: -c stops after the assembler: the result is an object file. It is not runnable because the linker has not yet resolved area and printf. -E gives preprocessed text and -S gives assembly.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Undefined behavior, and the tools that catch it
question: An ASan report says `heap-use-after-free ... READ of size 4 ... in main uaf.c:7` and `freed by thread T0 here: ... in main uaf.c:6`. What is the bug?
options: Line 7 reads through a pointer whose block was freed on line 6
Line 6 frees a pointer that malloc never returned
Line 7 reads an uninitialized local variable on the stack
The program ran out of heap memory
explain: ASan reports the bad access (line 7), plus where the block was freed (line 6) and allocated. Reading 4 bytes after free is a use after free. The fix is to finish using the data before freeing it, or not to free it yet.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Slices and why references cannot dangle
question: `let s = String::from("hello world"); let w = &s[6..11];` What does `w` hold?
options: A new heap allocation containing "world"
A pointer to byte 6 and length 11
A copy of the whole String header
A pointer to byte 6 of `s`'s buffer and length 5
explain: Slices never copy data. The range 6..11 starts at index 6 and stops before 11, so the length is 11 - 6 = 5, which is "world".

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: The dot product: one number that measures alignment
question: A search system ranks documents by raw dot product with the query embedding. Users complain that long, rambling documents always win. Which change most directly targets the cause?
options: Use more embedding dimensions
Square every dot product before ranking
Add a constant to every component of the query
Rank by cosine similarity, or normalize all embeddings to unit length
explain: If document vectors grow longer with document length, the dot product rewards that length. Dividing by the norms (cosine) keeps only direction. More dimensions or squaring the score keeps the length effect; adding a constant changes the query's direction, not the bias.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Loss: turning "fits the data" into one number
question: In the four-point example, you double every target $y_i$ (so the data look like $y = 4x$). Where does the minimum of the MSE move?
options: It stays at 1.99
It moves to 2.99
It moves to 3.98
It moves to 7.96
explain: $w^* = \sum x_i y_i / \sum x_i^2$. Doubling every $y_i$ doubles the numerator, so $w^* = 119.4 / 30 = 3.98$. The minimum loss quadruples too, since every residual doubles before squaring.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Why a single linear layer cannot learn XOR
question: A network has three hidden layers of 512 units each, but every activation is the identity. Which statement is true?
options: It can only represent affine functions of its input, same as a single linear layer
It can represent any continuous function given enough units
It can represent XOR but not more complex functions
It is equivalent to a single hidden layer network with ReLU
explain: Each layer is affine and the composition of affine maps is affine, so the whole stack collapses to $W'x+b'$. The extra parameters add cost but no expressive power.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Backprop in practice: cost, memory, vanishing gradients
question: You double the batch size and the run now goes out of GPU memory, even though the model's weights are unchanged. What is the most likely cause?
options: The weights are copied once per example
Backprop needs a second copy of the loss
Stored activations for the backward pass scale with batch size
Gradients scale with batch size while weights do not, and gradients are the bulk
explain: Weights and their gradients have a fixed size. Activations kept for the backward pass scale with batch size times depth, so they grow. Remedies: a smaller batch, gradient checkpointing (recompute instead of store), or lower precision activations.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Persistence: disks, inodes and crash-safe journaling
question: A crash leaves only the new inode I[v2] on disk; the bitmap B[v2] and data block Db were not written. What is the state?
options: Inconsistent: the inode points to a block the bitmap says is free, and that block holds old garbage
Consistent and correct: the inode is the source of truth
A harmless space leak
Lost data but a consistent file system
explain: The inode now points to the new data block (block 5 in OSTEP), but Db never reached it, so reading the file returns whatever was there before. The bitmap still says that block is free, contradicting the inode. This is the case fsck or journaling exists to prevent. Only-Db is the harmless case; only-bitmap is the leak.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Why averages are stable: the law of large numbers and the CLT
question: Batch size 64 gives a gradient-estimate standard deviation of s (per coordinate, i.i.d. examples). Approximately what does batch size 256 give?
options: s, since batch size does not affect noise
explain: The mini-batch gradient is an average of per-example gradients, so its standard deviation scales as 1/sqrt(batch). Four times the batch gives sqrt(4) = 2 times less noise, so s/2. The variance falls by 4.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Counting training compute: C is about 6ND
question: Your budget is fixed. You decide to make the model 3 times larger than planned. What must happen to the number of training tokens?
options: It stays the same, compute depends only on N
It must triple
It must drop to one third
It must drop to one ninth
explain: With $C \approx 6ND$ fixed, $D = C/(6N)$, so tripling N cuts D to one third. Compute depends on both knobs; nothing about the product is squared.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Why you need a test collection before you can say better
question: System D is a new dense retriever evaluated on an old pooled collection. 30% of its top-10 documents were never judged. With default trec_eval settings, what happens to those documents?
options: They are skipped, and precision is computed only over judged documents
They are counted as nonrelevant, which can make D look worse than it is
They are counted as relevant, since the system found them
trec_eval refuses to score the run until they are judged
explain: trec_eval treats documents missing from the qrels like judged-nonrelevant ones. Skipping them is only done with the -J flag, which its own help text warns against using casually. If D finds relevant documents the pool missed, it gets no credit, so its score is biased downward.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Why keyword match misses meaning and cross-encoders are too slow
question: Which property is what makes the bi-encoder's precomputation possible?
options: Its passage vector is a function of the passage alone
It uses cosine instead of dot product
It is a smaller model than a cross-encoder
It tokenizes the query and passage with the same vocabulary
explain: Precomputation needs the passage representation to be independent of the query. Cosine versus dot product, model size and vocabulary are all irrelevant to that; a cross-encoder can share vocabulary and still cannot precompute anything.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Why language models read subwords, not words or characters
question: A word-level model with a 50,000-word vocabulary meets the made-up product name "Zorblax" at inference. What happens?
options: It maps to the single unknown token, so the model cannot tell it apart from any other unknown word
It is split into characters automatically
It is added to the vocabulary on the fly
The model raises an error and stops
explain: A word-level vocabulary is fixed after training. Any word outside it becomes the shared `<unk>` id, losing its identity. Falling back to smaller pieces is exactly what a subword tokenizer adds; a pure word-level one has no such fallback.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Tradeoffs: vocab size, numbers, languages, glitch tokens, alternatives
question: On the toy corpus from lesson 2, (e, s) occurs 9 times; e occurs 17 times and s 9 times. (i, d) occurs 3 times; i and d occur 3 times each. Which pair does the WordPiece score pick first, and which does BPE pick?
options: Both pick (e, s)
WordPiece picks (i, d) with score 1/3; BPE picks (e, s) with count 9
WordPiece picks (e, s) with score 9/153; BPE picks (i, d)
Both pick (i, d)
explain: WordPiece: $9/(17 \cdot 9) \approx 0.059$ for (e, s) versus $3/(3 \cdot 3) \approx 0.333$ for (i, d), the highest of any pair since i and d only ever appear together. BPE ignores the individual frequencies and takes the raw top count, (e, s) with 9.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: BatchNorm, LayerNorm and dropout: train mode vs eval mode
question: You validate a model with BatchNorm but forget `model.eval()`. Validation accuracy changes when you change the validation batch size. Why?
options: Dropout is still active and BatchNorm is unaffected
The running averages are reset at every forward pass
Gradients are being computed during validation
BatchNorm normalizes with each validation batch's own statistics, so each prediction depends on the other examples in its batch
explain: In train mode BatchNorm uses the current batch mean and variance, so changing the batch composition or size changes each example's output. It also keeps updating the running statistics with validation data. In eval mode it uses the fixed running averages.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Building the graph: insertion and the neighbor heuristic
question: Which change increases index build time but leaves query-time cost per ef roughly the same?
options: Raising ef at query time
Raising ef_construction
Raising M
Raising the dimension d
explain: ef_construction only controls the beam width during inserts. M also raises query cost because every expanded node has more neighbors to score; d makes every distance more expensive; ef is the query knob itself.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Language models: decoding cuts the tail, scaling stalls
question: In the OPT-125m experiment, which change to the loop gave only minor degradation over generations?
options: Using beam search instead of sampling
Training for fewer epochs
Keeping a random 10% of the original real data in every generation
Generating a synthetic dataset twice as large
explain: Mixing real data back in each generation re-anchors the model to the true distribution. The paper reports only minor degradation in that setting, versus clear degradation with no original data.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: mmap: putting a file into your address space
question: You want to map a file starting at byte 5000. Page size is 4096. What do you pass, and where is byte 5000 in the result?
options: offset 5000; byte 5000 is at p[0]
offset 0; byte 5000 is at p[904]
offset 8192; byte 5000 is at p[-3192]
offset 4096; byte 5000 is at p[904]
explain: offset must be page-aligned, so round 5000 down to 4096 and add the remainder yourself: 5000 - 4096 = 904. Passing 5000 fails with EINVAL. Remember to extend length by the same 904 bytes so the end of the range you want is still covered.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Coordinated omission: the load tester stops looking when it hurts
question: Which change to a closed-loop tester does NOT fix coordinated omission?
options: Measuring each request from the time the schedule says it should have been sent
Sending requests on a fixed schedule from independent senders that never wait for responses
Adding more connections so that each one blocks less often
Back-filling the missing samples using a known expected interval between requests
explain: More connections reduce the effect but every connection still stops sending while it waits, so the bias remains (the NSDI paper notes closed systems approach open ones only slowly as concurrency grows). Measuring from intended start, open-loop sending, and interval-based back-fill all restore the missing samples.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Normalizing partial dates and Present against a reference date
question: Your normalizer computes *Present* using the server clock at index time. A profile indexed on 2025-01-15 with *Sep 2021 to Present* is searched on 2026-10-20. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, Present is stored as a string
Its tenure keeps growing, because tenure is recomputed at query time
The role is double counted
Its tenure is frozen at the index date and is about 21 months short
explain: Index-time resolution freezes Present to 2025-01, so tenure stops growing: Sep 2021 to Jan 2025 is 41 months, while at the query date it is 62. The role also stops counting as current. Store the open end and resolve it against the query's reference date, or re-index regularly.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Two ways to spend more compute on one prompt
question: Which method is **sequential** in the s1 paper's sense?
options: Majority vote over 64 independent samples
Best-of-N with unit tests
Letting the model keep reasoning after it tried to stop, so later tokens build on earlier ones
Running the same prompt on 8 GPUs at once
explain: Sequential means later computation depends on earlier computation, like a longer chain of thought or a revision. The other options are independent attempts (parallel) or just hardware parallelism.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Thinking longer: reasoning models and budget forcing
question: DeepSeek-R1-Zero's responses became much longer during RL even though no reward term asked for length. Why is that evidence for test-time scaling?
options: Longer outputs are always rewarded by GRPO
Length was capped at 1,000 tokens
The model copied long human traces
The reward was only for correctness and format, so the model discovered that spending more tokens per problem raised its success rate
explain: R1-Zero's rewards were rule-based accuracy and format rewards. Growth in thinking length alongside accuracy shows the policy learned to buy correctness with test-time tokens.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Making TTT fast: mini-batch gradient descent and the dual form
question: What does the dual form change about a TTT layer?
options: Its outputs: it is an approximation that trades accuracy for speed
Only how the same outputs are computed: matmuls replace per-token outer products, and the intermediate G_t and W_t are never stored
The loss: it switches from reconstruction to a dot-product loss
The order of updates: it processes tokens right to left
explain: The paper stresses that primal and dual forms are equivalent in output. The dual form spends a bit more theoretical compute (an extra O(b^2 d) term) to get matmul-friendly operations and avoid materializing b matrices of size d x d.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: The magazine: a per-CPU stack of object pointers
question: CPU 2 only frees packet buffers; CPU 5 only allocates them. With magazines and a depot, how do buffers get from CPU 2 to CPU 5?
options: Each buffer goes back to the slab layer, then CPU 5 takes it from there
CPU 5 steals single objects from CPU 2's magazine under CPU 2's lock
CPU 2 returns full magazines to the depot and CPU 5 loads them, moving M buffers per depot visit
They cannot: each CPU's objects are private forever
explain: Whole magazines are the unit of exchange. The freeing CPU fills magazines and swaps them for empties at the depot; the allocating CPU swaps empties for those full ones. The depot lock is taken about once per M objects on each side.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: Why memory is becoming a hierarchy of tiers
question: Using the model with DRAM 100 ns and CXL 200 ns, what fraction of accesses must hit DRAM to get an average of 120 ns?
explain: 120 = 100h + 200(1 minus h) = 200 minus 100h, so h = 0.8. Each 1% of accesses moved to CXL adds 1 ns here.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Splitting a series into trend, season and remainder
question: A city's electricity demand used to peak in winter (heating) and now peaks in summer (air conditioning). Which decomposition choice handles this best?
options: Classical decomposition, because it averages each month over all years
A larger moving-average window for the trend
STL with a seasonal component allowed to change over time
Multiplicative classical decomposition
explain: Classical decomposition assumes the same seasonal pattern every year, so it would average the old winter peak with the new summer peak. STL lets the seasonal component evolve, which is exactly what this series needs. FPP3 uses this electricity example to illustrate the limitation.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: From threads to blocks: the Triton programming model
question: A Triton program loads a block of 1024 floats and is compiled with num_warps=4. How many hardware threads share that block?
options: 1, because Triton programs are single-threaded
32, one warp
128, so on average 8 values per thread
1024, one per value
explain: num_warps=4 means 4 x 32 = 128 threads cooperate on one program instance. The 1024 values are spread over them, 8 per thread on average. The single-threaded view is how you write the code, not how it runs.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Autotuning, num_warps, num_stages and when to use Triton
question: A kernel is autotuned with key=["M", "N", "K"]. You call it 1000 times with M = N = K = 4096, then once with K = 8192. How many times does it benchmark the full config list?
options: Once, on the very first call only
Twice: on the first 4096 call and on the first call with K = 8192
1001 times, once per call
Never, configs are chosen at import time
explain: Autotuning reruns whenever the values of the key arguments change. The first 4096 call benchmarks and caches the winner, the next 999 reuse it, and the new K value triggers one more round.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Continuous images: one transformer, two losses
question: Why does capping the diffusion noise at t = 500 for image-before-caption pairs help captioning?
options: The caption tokens attend to the image, and with full noise they would often be describing near-pure noise
It halves the number of image tokens
It makes the image loss computed per token instead of per image
It switches the image to discrete tokens
explain: In training the image is noised for its own diffusion loss, and later tokens condition on that noisy version. When the caption follows the image, a heavily noised image hides the content to describe. Limiting noise keeps the image readable; the paper measured better CIDEr with under 1% effect elsewhere.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Booting on the hypervisor: virtual devices, boot time and memory
question: A unikernel's guest boot takes 0.3 ms and total VM start takes 40 ms on standard QEMU. What will most reduce cold-start latency?
options: Removing more micro-libraries from the image
Using a faster memory allocator
Moving from KVM to emulation mode
Switching to a lightweight VMM such as Firecracker or Solo5
explain: The guest is under 1% of the 40 ms. Unikraft's measurements put total boot at about 3 ms on Firecracker and Solo5 versus about 40 ms on QEMU, so the VMM choice is the lever.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: SIMD distance kernels: lanes, FMA and the horizontal sum
question: hnswlib builds an inner-product index with d = 100. Which kernel does it pick on an AVX machine?
options: The SIMD16 kernel with a 4-element scalar tail
The pure scalar loop
The SIMD4 kernel, since 100 is a multiple of 4
The AVX-512 kernel with a masked tail
explain: The dispatch checks d % 16 first, then d % 4. 100 is not a multiple of 16 but is a multiple of 4, so the SIMD4 kernel covers all 100 elements with no tail. The residual kernels are used only when neither divides d.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: WorkerGroups, resource pools and DataProto dispatch
question: Two roles are mapped to the same ResourcePool and fused with create_colocated_worker_cls. What is the main effect?
options: Both roles run in one Ray actor per GPU and share one CUDA and distributed context
Both roles get disjoint halves of the pool's GPUs
The roles run concurrently on the GPU with separate memory pools
The roles are forced to use the same model weights
explain: Same pool means same GPUs; fusing the classes avoids one process per role per GPU. The roles still run one after another in the order the controller calls them. Disjoint GPUs require different pools.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Why an hour of video does not fit: frames times tokens
question: Which statement about 8-frame uniform sampling of a 1-hour video is correct?
options: It is fine because the vision encoder sees all frames before sampling
It costs 8 x 196 = 1,568 visual tokens but leaves 7.5-minute gaps the model never sees
It is equivalent to 1 fps sampling with 2 x 2 pooling
It fails only because the LLM context is too short
explain: Sampling happens before the encoder, so unsampled frames are never encoded. 3,600 s / 8 = 450 s between samples. The context is not the issue at 1,568 tokens; the missing information is.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Bigger context or captions: LongVA, Gemini 1.5, retrieval, benchmarks
question: A support team asks many questions about the same 2-hour screen recording, often about exact error codes shown briefly on screen. Which design fits best?
options: 8 uniformly sampled frames with 2 x 2 pooling
Caption retrieval over 5-second clips alone, since captions are cheap
Index the clips once, retrieve candidate moments per question, then re-inspect those frames at full resolution with a VLM
MovieChat global mode with a 256-frame long-term memory
explain: Many questions favor a reusable index. Brief, small on-screen text is exactly what pooling, merging and generic captions lose, so the retrieved moments need a full-resolution second look.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: The dynamics model: next-frame tokens with MaskGIT
question: Why does Genie train the dynamics model with masking rates drawn between 0.5 and 1 rather than always masking just the last frame completely?
options: To make training cheaper by skipping tokens
Because MaskGIT decoding starts from a heavily masked frame and refines partially filled ones, so training must cover many masking levels
To hide the latent actions from the model
To make the tokenizer's codebook smaller
explain: At inference each frame goes from fully masked to fully filled through intermediate states. Training on a range of masking rates teaches the model to predict masked tokens from the partial context it will see at every iteration.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Where ViT-B/16's 86 million parameters live
question: A colleague proposes ViT-B with 16 heads instead of 12 (D stays 768) to get more capacity. How does the parameter count of a block change?
options: It stays the same: each head gets 48 dims instead of 64
It grows by one third, since each head has its own Q, K, V
It doubles, because attention cost is quadratic
It shrinks, because the MLP gets smaller
explain: Multi-head attention splits the D = 768 output columns of Q, K and V among the heads. With 16 heads each head has 768 / 16 = 48 dims; the matrices are still 768 x 768. More heads changes how capacity is used, not how many weights exist.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: From a VLM that describes to a VLA that acts
question: During a robot task, RT-2 restricts decoding to valid action tokens only. What failure does this prevent?
options: The model running out of GPU memory
Cross-entropy loss becoming negative
The model answering with ordinary words that cannot be turned into a robot command
Image tokens being emitted as output
explain: RT-2 must output something executable. Constraining the output vocabulary to the 256 action tokens on robot prompts guarantees a parsable action, while the same model still answers normal vision-language questions with full text.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: Running action chunks in the control loop
question: You must control a 14-dim bimanual robot at 50 Hz for laundry folding, where demonstrators fold in different orders. Which action head fits best?
options: Per-step 256-bin tokens, since it needs no extra modules
Mean-squared-error regression of one action per step
A flow-matching action expert that outputs 50-step chunks
Per-step tokens with a larger vocabulary
explain: Per-step tokens would need 700 tokens per second; regression averages different folding strategies. A flow-matching expert produces continuous 50-step chunks in one short loop and samples one mode, which is what pi0 was built for.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: VQGAN: perceptual and adversarial losses for 256-token images
question: A VQGAN's adversarial loss starts dominating training and reconstructions drift away from the input. Which part of the method is designed to prevent this?
options: The commitment loss weight beta
The straight-through estimator
The adaptive weight lambda, computed from gradient norms at the last decoder layer
The sliding attention window used at sampling time
explain: lambda = grad of L_rec / (grad of L_GAN + delta) at the last decoder layer. When the GAN gradient grows relative to the reconstruction gradient, lambda falls, scaling the adversarial term down.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: One attention layer, many kernels: the backend abstraction
question: Which piece declares that a backend needs compute capability 8.0 or higher?
options: The `AttentionImpl` instance, by checking the GPU inside `forward`
The metadata builder, by raising during `build()`
The `AttentionBackend` class, through `supports_compute_capability`, which selection calls before anything runs
The scheduler, which skips requests on unsupported GPUs
explain: Capabilities live on the backend class so they can be checked at startup. `validate_configuration` calls `supports_compute_capability` along with the head size, dtype, KV dtype and block size checks.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Turning an image into tokens a language model can read
question: A ViT with 14 x 14 patches runs on a 448 x 448 input with no pooling. How many patch tokens does it produce?
explain: $448 / 14 = 32$ patches per side, and $32 \cdot 32 = 1024$. 32 is only the side length, and 576 is the count for 336 x 336 input. Token count grows with the square of the side length.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Reading a receipt into validated JSON
question: Which extraction error would the two arithmetic checks in this lesson NOT catch?
options: A unit price misread from 8.75 as 3.75
The merchant name misread as a similar name
A subtotal misread from 21.55 as 27.55
A total misread from 23.27 as 28.27
explain: Price, subtotal and total errors all break one of the sums. The merchant name takes part in no arithmetic, so it needs another check, such as matching against a known merchant list, or human review.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: A practical wait-free queue: phases and helping (Kogan-Petrank)
question: A thread on an otherwise idle 64-thread system calls `enq()` on the base Kogan-Petrank queue. Roughly how much work does it do?
options: Constant work, like the Michael-Scott queue
Work proportional to 64, because maxPhase() and help() each scan the whole state array
Unbounded work, since helping can repeat forever
Work proportional to the queue length
explain: Even with no contention the base version reads every descriptor twice: once to compute the phase and once in help(). The paper's optimizations replace maxPhase() with an atomic counter and make help() check one or a few entries per call in cyclic order, which keeps the bound but cuts the uncontended cost.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Inside the models: a multimesh GNN and a 3D Earth transformer
question: Why does GraphCast run its 16 processor layers on a multimesh instead of directly on the 721 x 1440 grid with nearest-neighbor edges?
options: Because GNNs cannot represent grids
Because the multimesh has more nodes than the grid, giving higher resolution
With only local edges, 16 layers move information only about 16 cells, and the lat-lon grid is very uneven near the poles
Because the multimesh lets the model skip the decoder
explain: Each message-passing layer moves information one edge. Long coarse-level edges let a few layers reach across the globe, and the icosahedral mesh is near-uniform. The mesh has fewer nodes (40,962) than the grid (about 1 million).

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Why a pool needs more than one shared queue
question: Which workload gains the most from work stealing over static per-worker queues?
options: Millions of identical 1 ms tasks dealt evenly to workers
A single long task that cannot be split
Tasks that each hold a global lock for their whole run
A recursive divide-and-conquer job whose subproblems vary wildly in size
explain: Stealing fixes imbalance. Evenly dealt identical tasks have none, one unsplittable task cannot be shared, and a global lock serializes everything anyway. Uneven recursive work is exactly where idle workers find something to steal.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Parking idle workers without lost wakeups or thundering herds
question: A pool notifies a parked worker on every single push. A burst of 1,000 tasks arrives on one worker with 15 workers parked. What is the main problem?
options: Tasks are executed twice
All 15 workers can be woken at once and pile onto the same victim queue, and many go back to sleep empty-handed
Tasks are lost because the futex only wakes one thread
Nothing; more wakeups always help
explain: That is the thundering herd the Tokio 0.1 scheduler suffered. Waking only when nobody is searching, and letting each successful searcher wake the next, brings workers online one at a time as they find work.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Cheap scaling studies, continual training and failure modes
question: You must produce models at 4 data sizes for each of 5 model sizes. Which plan uses WSD correctly to minimize compute?
options: 20 runs from scratch, each with WSD and a 10% cooldown
1 run of the largest model, with cooldowns used to simulate the smaller models
5 cosine runs with T equal to the longest length, evaluated at 4 intermediate checkpoints
5 long constant-LR runs (one per size), each with 4 cooldown branches from checkpoints
explain: Cooldowns replace the data axis, not the model axis: each model size still needs its own trunk. The cosine-checkpoint option is the classic mistake, since mid-run cosine checkpoints are not annealed and underestimate those lengths.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: MSG_ZEROCOPY: sending from your own memory safely
question: A program sends with MSG_ZEROCOPY and gets notification [7, 9] with SO_EE_CODE_ZEROCOPY_COPIED set. What does it know?
options: Sends 7, 8 and 9 were delivered to the peer
Buffers for sends 7, 8 and 9 may be reused, and the kernel ended up copying their data
Only send 9 completed; 7 and 8 are still pinned
Sends 7 to 9 failed and must be retried
explain: The range is inclusive, so ids 7, 8 and 9 are released. The COPIED code says the data went out via a copy, so zero-copy brought no benefit for them; it does not signal failure. Neither part means delivery: a notification is about page ownership, not about the peer.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Prompting an LLM and calibrating its label bias
question: For a 4-label prompt, the content-free probabilities come out as (0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25). What does contextual calibration change?
options: It sharpens every prediction toward the top label
Nothing: W is 4 times the identity, which keeps the argmax and, after renormalizing, the probabilities
It flips the ranking of the top two labels
It sets every prediction to uniform
explain: W = diag(1/0.25) = 4I, which scales every label equally. The argmax cannot change and renormalized probabilities are unchanged. Calibration only matters when the prompt has a bias, which is exactly when p_cf is not uniform.
